title: IS FERNANDO MENDOZA THE NEXT BRADY? OR IS HE TOO "LINKEDIN" TO RULE THE NFL?
text:
IS FERNANDO MENDOZA THE NEXT BRADY? OR IS HE TOO “LINKEDIN” TO RULE THE NFL?
This is an important juncture in Brady’s post-QB career, when he drafts a player with the magic to win a Heisman and lead Indiana to a 16-0 season — but can Mendoza excel in a pressurized situation?
The day will come when he dumps his naive LinkedIn posture, which makes him appear prepared for ceremonial knighthood. Does Fernando Mendoza realize he’ll play quarterback for the damnable Raiders, in Sin City, with drugs and casinos and blinding lights and naked women by the pool and Maxx Crosby still screaming in the locker room?
Maybe it happens tonight, when he watches Tom Brady select him as the overall No. 1 draft pick in a relationship that should hit home. Mendoza is why Brady wanted to become an NFL minority owner and why he should ditch his Fox Sports gig. This should remind the rookie that he’s the GOAT’s pupil, with an expectation that he’ll become an all-time great.
Is such a whim actually possible? Mendoza taking over as an American myth? He was delightful as a collegian, dropping tears on sidelines and leading Indiana to an unthinkable 16-0 season. Shouldn’t we question if he’s green, unfinished? “Hopefully I can update my LinkedIn on April 23,” he said, smiling as usual, “when I go from unemployed to employed.”
Because he knows what awaits him in Las Vegas. Brady is burning as a 3-14 loser who hasn’t replaced Troy Aikman as the finest network analyst. He won his seven Super Bowls and must win another as an executive. Good luck to Mendoza when he is greeted within a quarterback room like no other. If he thought Curt Cignetti drove him mad, wait until Brady picks up a football at 48 and heaves it better than almost everyone in the league.
“He gave me the message that he’s going to push me, and he’s not going to be all lovey-dovey,” he said of Brady. “He’s going to be a mentor.”
The draft begins in Pittsburgh, a town that is wiping graffiti off bridges and would love to hear Aaron Rodgers confirm he’s returning — when he’s still a postseason rat. Mendoza will not be in the city, preferring to be in his hometown of Miami with his mother, Elsa. She has been fighting multiple sclerosis for almost 20 years. It is far more important to celebrate his anointment with family than in front of Steel City lunatics.
“My mom really wanted to do it at home,” Mendoza said. “It’s a lot easier for us with the family situation. I see her fighting every single day, and with a smile on her face. So there’s no excuse for me to have a bad day, a bad play or a bad game. I’m always trying to have an optimistic approach, give the best and serve the best to my teammates.
“We need to hop on a plane the next day, and to be there with the village that’s poured into me — friends, family, coaches, mentors — and to be there with all of them and to share the start of this journey. It’s going to create the best memory for our family.”
His attitude is what makes people root for him. His first NFL commercial is with Pfizer, starting tonight, when he’ll demand early cancer screenings. We will survey his summer sessions and wonder if he’ll beat out Kirk Cousins, a veteran who was acquired if Mendoza isn’t ready. “I think it does help the player if they can sit behind a mature adult and watch how they run the show,” said Klint Kubiak, the new head coach. “He’s a national champion, he’s a winner, he’s accurate, he’s strong, he’s tall, he’s intelligent.”
But he’s raw. “The best guy will play,” said John Spytek, the so-called general manager when Brady is traveling each week. “Ultimately, this is a meritocracy. It’s just really hard to play really well at a young age. But we’ve seen plenty of quarterbacks do it recently.”
Is he Joe Burrow? Caleb Williams? Or Bryce Young? Or a backup to Cousins, who will play if Brady and Kubiak think time is needed? The Heisman Trophy means nothing.
“I’m putting all of my efforts toward just trying to be the best quarterback possible for the season,” Mendoza said. “But I know at the next level, there’s going to be a lot more snaps under center and that’s a big adjustment. I need to get used to that and just the nature of the game. Not only that, the hashmarks are more condensed and the speed of the game is faster. So all those things, I look forward to learning.”
Remember, he wasn’t recruited much in high school. He went to Yale until choosing Cal. No one knew him when he showed up in Bloomington. His rise, with Cignetti’s, is historic. He viewed the last three months as a job search. “It’s been long, but it’s been great because a job interview usually is a couple of weeks or a single day in the office, but this interview has been a couple of months,” he said. “The teams know everything about you, and that’s been my favorite part. They can peel back the layers and see the true you.”
Will the true Mendoza be the true Brady? We have arrived at a juncture where the GOAT, nearing 50, needs a bigger form of success. He doesn’t need to sit with Kevin Burkhardt and lead cheers in the booth. He needs a passer he can describe as his own.
###
Jay Mariotti, called “without question the most impacting Chicago sportswriter of the past quarter-century,’’ writes general sports columns for Substack while appearing on some of the 1,678,498 podcasts and shows in production today. He is an accomplished columnist, TV panelist and talk/podcast host. Living in Los Angeles, he gravitated by osmosis to film projects.
